analysis.title: The Commodities Feed: Oil slides on easing Middle East tensions
key_insights: Brent fell below $92/bbl and WTI traded around $86/bbl on 10 November 2026 as the market unwound part of the geopolitical risk premium on expectations of US-Iran de-escalation.
Persian Gulf crude exports are estimated to have recovered to about 80-85% of pre-war levels including pipeline volumes. Refined product shipments are at roughly 35-40%.
Reports that Iran may soften its position on control of the Strait of Hormuz reduced concerns about a prolonged disruption.
China's October crude imports rose 13% month-on-month to about 42mt (9.9m b/d), helped by Persian Gulf recovery and stronger Iraqi volumes, but were still about 13% below year-ago levels.

Infrastructure risk persists: Ukrainian attacks on Russian refining capacity continue alongside Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy system. A fire on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was contained without a significant flow interruption.
ING expects oil to stay sensitive to Middle East developments because regional negotiations remain uncertain and infrastructure risks persist.
Henry Hub rose more than 8% to above $3.2/MMBtu on colder eastern US forecasts, short covering and stronger LNG feedgas demand, including at Freeport LNG.
US gas inventories rose 77Bcf last week, slightly less than expected, taking stocks to 3.801Tcf, about 2.8% below the same point last year.
Front-month TTF traded around €81/MWh, lower as Hormuz flow concerns eased.
Spot gold hovered around $4,100/oz, pressured by expectations of tighter US monetary policy. The prospect of another Fed rate hike is the key near-term headwind.
Lower oil prices have eased some of the inflation concerns that had supported expectations for tighter policy.

China's central bank added to gold reserves in October, extending its buying streak to 12 consecutive months. ING remains constructive on gold over the medium term but sees near-term pressure from higher US rates and a stronger dollar.

sector_views.rationale: Oil is losing geopolitical premium as Gulf flows recover, but ING expects continued sensitivity to Middle East developments and infrastructure disruptions.
